articles.title: Trump’s threats are now just saber-rattling with a plastic knife
articles.summary: In an opinion piece, Joslin Joseph argues that President Donald Trump’s second-term threats against allies and adversaries have lost their effectiveness due to a lack of administrative restraint.
articles.body:
The presidency’s power and mystique has surrounded every president, especially when the U.S. started to become a superpower. Building off President Theodore Roosevelt’s proverb of “speaking softly and carrying a big stick,” presidents over the decades have learned that the office commands respect. Speaking to our enemies, antagonists and wayward allies carried a considerable amount of gravity.

Unfortunately, President Trump has turned the power of the presidency into a joke. Trump has always been a blowhard — not just in real life, but also on reality TV, talk shows and Twitter. People flocked to him because he said the things everyone wanted politicians to say. In an age where politicians overanalyze every word in every speech, he was an off-the-cuff guy who would tell it like it is. And when people didn’t listen, he threatened them.

Coming into his second term, Trump ratcheted up the tough talk. He had the House, Senate and Supreme Court to back him up. He had carte blanche to carry out his very specific ideals on how to change the country, the presidency and his bank account. At first, it seemed to work. Trump would make demands and threats against, say, NATO, whose nations boosted their spending and its secretary general called him “daddy.” Businesses rolled back DEI programs, universities made settlements to be left alone by the administration, and television networks changed their programming because of his threats.

Lately, however, it seems that people are tired of being bullied. Trump’s threats are now as empty as a drained reflecting pool. Everyone from enemies, allies, political opponents, businesses and ordinary citizens have learned to tune him out or write him off as a wacko.

Take Iran. Trump and his administration are now praying that their new approach, Operation Economic Outcast will get Iran to fold. It turns out that the constant threats of bombings, destruction and death by Trump to the Iranians didn’t make them rush to the negotiating table. Instead, they chose to wait us out. We are now the ones panicking because of oil prices, economic fallout, and a dwindling supply of interceptors.

Canada went elbows up after Trump decided to initiate another pointless trade war. They are laughing at him up north and are ready to handle any fallout from our now fractured friendship. How badly did Trump’s threats of tariffs fail? He is now trying to convince us that changing the name of a lake will actually accomplish something.

One of the reasons Trump had success in his first term was that his threats and bluster were restrained by sensible people in his administration. They realized that someone who never thought about the fallout of his words should in fact rein it in from time to time. The effect was when Trump did threaten people, he came across as a no-nonsense president who wasn’t scared of offending people. Hence why his base loved him so much.

But as we all know, the Trump administration is now full of yes-men, sycophants, and overly zealous personal assistants who can’t or won’t stand up to the president when he goes off the rails. In fact, some have learned to echo his threats and stances even if it makes them look incompetent or foolish. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is a very accomplished businessman. But his tough talk on Iran and the sanctions didn’t make anyone shake in their boots.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has long parroted Trump’s vision of the military, ranting about lethality and being harsh on troops that didn’t fit their vision. Of course, Hegseth should have focused on logistics instead of lethality. If he had, the Iran war might be going better.

Presidents have always relied on the projection of power to talk tough. President Ronald Reagan famously told the Soviets to “tear down this wall” and people loved him for it. He was tough but restrained. He didn’t threaten the Soviets with annihilation if they didn’t. He did not have to. George W. Bush didn’t fly off the rails after the attacks on 9/11. He kept his messaging stern and focused and told us what we needed to expect. Even when he made the mistake of invading Iraq, he restrained himself lest it make him and this country look worse.

But now, we don’t have restraint. We have a president who cannot handle his emotions and has beefed with everyone from Pope Leo to Minnesota kindergarteners . And we have learned for better or worse to just ignore him. What is worse is our enemies are now learning to ignore him as well.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary-Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq.

articles.title: El-Sayed torched online after uneasy union member struggles through campaign event
articles.summary: A UAW worker's struggle at Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate press conference sparked a fierce debate between conservative and liberal commentators on X.
articles.body: A woman delivering remarks at a news conference held by Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Monday appeared visibly nervous and repeatedly paused during her speech, prompting a wave of speculation on social media about the reason for her unease. The woman, whom El-Sayed's staff identified as a union member employed by a truck factory, paused at multiple points during her speech, was breathing heavily and appeared uneasy. El-Sayed and Democratic State Sen. Mallory McMorrow both attempted to comfort the woman as she trudged through her remarks. Some conservative commentators on social media questioned whether the woman had been coerced into speaking at the event, while others used the moment to criticize El-Sayed's campaign organization. These claims drew the ire of Mallory McMorrow, who ran against El-Sayed in the state’s Democratic primary but has since endorsed his candidacy. "She had never spoken at a press conference before. Beforehand, she shared with me that she was really nervous. articles.body:
Hunter Biden on Monday said former Vice President Kamala Harris was not “loyal to a fault” to his father, former President Biden.

The president’s son sat for an interview in Los Angeles with Zeteo Editor-in-Chief Mehdi Hasan for a wide-ranging conversation about President Biden’s time in office, his handling of the Israel-Hamas war and Harris as vice president.

Hasan pressed that Hunter Biden’s criticisms of Harris could be seen “as throwing her under the bus,” prompting Hunter Biden to reply, “Oh, boy,” before laughing.

“Let me just state it exactly clearly. I think that she was loyal to my father, and I don’t think that she was loyal to a fault, however,” he later said.

Hasan pressed Hunter Biden on this, who said “people” would tell him that Harris “was so loyal to your dad.”

“Well,” Hunter Biden said he would reply, “maybe from your perspective, but maybe not from mine.”

“How is she not loyal to your dad?” Hasan replied, to which Hunter Biden said, “That’s between me and her.”

The president’s son defended not expanding further on the divide between him and Harris, saying he “ain’t running for anything” and he can “say whatever the f‑‑‑ I want.”

He said he sees Harris having a “deep, rich future in politics, whether she wants to run for president again, she’ll be –– not the frontrunner. But she’s not a very good politician.”

Hunter Biden, who has made a slew of media appearances and has been on a posting spree on social media, last month called Harris “not a very good politician.”

“I don’t see how she possibly thinks that distancing herself from Joe Biden is even possible,” he told the “Amped Up” podcast. “And why would you, if you really believed in the record that you had left?”

Harris replaced Joe Biden at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024 after Democratic lawmakers and donors, including actor George Clooney and former President Obama, called on the president to step aside following a disastrous debate performance with President Trump.

She is among the possible contenders for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

Harris at times critiqued the Trump administration, having revamped her social media campaign to advocate for Democratic causes and mock Trump and the White House.

Some Democrats are split on her involvement in the 2026 midterms, with some saying she is a liability while others, including Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) in his reelection effort, have expressed gratitude for her support.

Harris herself has also been critical of some facets of the Biden administration, including Joe Biden himself. She wrote in her campaign memoir, “107 Days,” that his decision to run for reelection amounted to “ recklessness ” and accused his staffers of “ adding fuel ” to negative stories about her.

articles.body:
A slew of stars — including “Star Wars” actor Mark Hamill, Jesse Eisenberg, “The West Wing” actor Dulé Hill and Bernadette Peters — are bringing a classic animated film to life in a show of support for immigrant communities.

The entertainers will perform a live reading of the 1986 film “An American Tail,” at a Sept. 10 virtual benefit hosted by the Workers Circle.

The Jewish social justice organization said the star-studded reading is part of its “ongoing efforts to defend this country’s immigrant communities during President Trump’s second term and to build a more just and inclusive democracy.”

“An American Tail” follows the story of a 19th century mouse named Fievel, as the pip squeak-sized protagonist immigrates from the Russian Empire with his Jewish family in the hopes of a brighter future in the United States.

The movie was chosen, the Workers Circle said in a statement, because at “a moment when immigrant communities across the country face increased threats of detention, deportation and family separation, the hopes and struggles at the heart of ‘An American Tail’ remain deeply relevant.”

Richard Kind, “West Side Story” actor Josh Andrés Rivera, “The Devil Wears Prada 2” star Tracie Thoms and actor Malky Goldman are also poised to participate in the benefit. Tickets for the non-profit’s fundraiser range from $18 to $72.

According to data released last month by the Deportation Data Project, Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained almost 50,000 people in July. The number marks the highest monthly arrest total during the president’s second term.

articles.title: Democrats blink in shutdown fight, hand Trump and GOP win before midterms
articles.summary: House Democrats caved on their government shutdown push, but conservatives raged over a hemp ban delay and federal grants provision in the CR.
articles.body: House Democrats relented to Republicans in their quest to prevent a government shutdown after spending months raising the possibility ahead of the crucial midterm elections. Tuesday’s successful vote in the House, the second such attempt since July, means that lawmakers have officially punted funding the government until after the November election and are sending the short-term funding patch, known as a continuing resolution (CR), to President Donald Trump’s desk. It also marks the end of months of concerns that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would again shut the government down for political gain as they vie for control of Congress. DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE Both top Democrats caved on pushing for another shutdown, for now. And that gave House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who needed Democratic votes to pass the bill, a win. But while House Democrats agreed to support the bipartisan CR that passed the Senate last month, conservatives raged about certain changes that negotiators in the upper chamber wove into the bill. Conservatives were outraged over an unrelated measure to delay a congressionally approved hemp product ban by 30 days and a provision curbing the Trump administration’s control over federal grants. TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., and members of Johnson’s right flank have criticized the CR over the hemp ban delay and grant rule change, a sentiment shared by Republicans in the Senate. "The Senate did violence to our bill," Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "Hemp and the grants are the two big ones…and frankly, I just don’t think CRs ought to be on suspension…when you put it on suspension, you’re not asking for my vote, okay, you’re going to get Democrats." Voting on a bill under "suspension" means it gets fast-tracked past multiple procedural hurdles in exchange for raising the threshold for passage from a simple majority to two-thirds. But the modification to the grant rule doesn’t permanently kill it. SCHUMER CAVES, HANDS REPUBLICANS SHUTDOWN WIN AFTER MONTHS OF UNCERTAINTY Senate Republicans were assured by the administration that the push for more control over federal grants could be ready to go by the time the stopgap expires in December. Democrats argue it could be used as a tool to dictate which states do and don't get federal dollars. Meanwhile, the CR punts the deadline to avert a government shutdown to Dec. 11, giving lawmakers a little over a month to create a new federal budget for fiscal year 2027, which begins Oct. 1. But House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., whose panel is in charge of writing those spending bills along with its Senate counterpart, told Fox News Digital that would not be enough time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He placed blame squarely on Senate Democrats, who he argued were trying to hinder Senate Appropriations Committee Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, and her bid for re-election come November. "They clearly do not want Susan Collins to have any success. So all of America has to suffer until they figure out who's going to win in Maine," Cole said. "We're going to risk a year-long CR, if not a shutdown. So they've just been incredibly irresponsible."

articles.title: House passes short-term funding bill to prevent a shutdown before the election
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The House voted Tuesday to pass a short-term funding bill and avert a government shutdown at the end of September, keeping money flowing at current levels until Dec. 11.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The House voted Tuesday to pass a short-term funding bill and avert a government shutdown at the end of September, keeping money flowing at current levels until Dec. 11. The legislation, which has already passed the Senate, sailed through the chamber by a vote of 370-48. It now goes to President Donald Trump, who is expected to sign it. That would take the biggest legislative item off the to-do list for Congress ahead of the elections Nov. 3, punting stalled negotiations over a full-year funding deal until after the midterms. The two parties have clashed over the scope of federal spending as Democrats reject Trump’s call for a massive $1.5 trillion military budget, a spike from the already record-breaking $1 trillion that Congress gave the military this year. Funding the government requires 60 Senate votes to defeat a filibuster, meaning it must have bipartisan support even though Republicans control both chambers and the White House. House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole, R-Okla., accused Democrats of blocking a deal to weaken politically vulnerable Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee. “I do want to finish all the bills before the end of the year. Now, whether we can do that or not is another matter,” Cole said, referring to the 12 appropriations bills that fund the government. “We won’t know if we’ll be doing that till after the election.” The winners of the midterm elections will feel empowered to press their demands in the lame-duck negotiations, knowing that they’ll have more power in the upcoming year. The election “has a tremendous impact,” Cole said. “We will act like we can come back and things will be exactly the way they were when we left. They won’t be. Everybody’s calculations will change. Everybody’s point of view will change. It’ll have an enormous impact about what happens for the balance of the year.” Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., said she hopes to become chair of the Appropriations Committee again if Democrats win the House. But she said her only priority now is to finalize a full government funding deal for the new fiscal year before 2027 begins. “The midterm election will have an effect, but the goal is that we need to pass appropriations bills before the end of the year. That is a bipartisan view of where we need to go with the committee, and so that’s what we are going to press for,” DeLauro said. “Let’s get to the finish line.”

articles.title: Congress funds government until December, averting preelection shutdown
articles.summary: The House on Tuesday voted to send a short-term extension of government funding to President Trump’s desk, avoiding a politically risky shutdown before the midterm elections. The continuing resolution (CR), which funds the government through Dec. 11, passed the House on a 370-48 vote, with 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats voting in opposition. The Senate…
articles.body:
The House on Tuesday voted to send a short-term extension of government funding to President Trump’s desk, avoiding a politically risky shutdown before the midterm elections.

The continuing resolution (CR), which funds the government through Dec. 11, passed the House on a 370-48 vote, with 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats voting in opposition. The Senate advanced the measure by a landslide last month .

The CR now pushes the spending battle to before the holidays, when the outcome of the midterms will help determine how much leverage each party holds to set the spending agenda.

It’s rare for Congress to pass a CR this early in the year, almost a month before funding expires on Sept. 30 — even as political polarization has made finding bipartisan consensus on funding increasingly difficult and CRs necessary to keep the government open.

But the early timeline and the broad bipartisan support the CR received are clear signals that both parties were anxious to avoid a fall funding fight with the congressional majority hanging in the balance. Congress has contended with two record-breaking shutdowns in the past year alone.

The Senate version of the CR was adopted by a margin of 90-6, and several of the Democratic senators who voted “no” did so as a signal, as they knew the bill would succeed without them.

Still, the funding stopgap didn’t get universal support in the House, and it could cause problems for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.).

Some hard-line Republicans voted against the CR — and voted against a rule for four unrelated bills — because of objections to provisions the Senate had added, including a short-term delay of a ban on intoxicating hemp products. The White House and the cannabis industry want to delay a congressionally enacted ban for a month to negotiate a different deal, but many Republicans want the ban to kick in as planned.

Some are also not thrilled with a provision that temporarily blocks a rule that would reshape how the Trump administration disperses federal grants by giving more power to political appointees in distributing federal funds.

House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) said avoiding a shutdown was worth the complaints.

“When we passed our continuing resolution over here, we knew it would change when it got to the Senate,” Cole said on the floor just before the vote. “Some of those changes I actually agree with, some of them I don’t. But they don’t really change the substance of the fact we bought the time that we need to get through the election cycle and hopefully the time that we need to get down to serious bargaining on the other side of it.”

Democrats have generally not been inclined to back government funding resolutions during Trump’s second term. But the grantmaking provision added by the Senate, coupled with a desire to prevent a funding lapse, brought many Democrats on board.

On Tuesday morning, House Democrats huddled behind closed doors in the Capitol basement for their first all-caucus, in-person meeting since the House left Washington in July for the long summer break. Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the senior Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, made the case for supporting the funding package. “That’s a big statement from the ranking member. She’s my ranking member, so I have a tough time disagreeing with her,” quipped Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chair of the House Democratic Caucus and a member of the Appropriations panel. Others jumped on board, even as some of them bashed the process of funding the government on a temporary basis. Rep. Ted Lieu (Calif.), the vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, noted the shutdown deadline is not until Oct. 1 and argued that Congress should work to come up with a longer-term package. “We have a whole nother month left, and the Republicans who control the House, the Senate and the White House are basically waving the white flag of surrender and saying, ‘We don’t know how to govern, we don’t know how to pass appropriations bills,’” Lieu told reporters in the Capitol. “It is not a good way to run our federal government. But it’s the only alternative that’s going to be before us, so I’ll be voting for it.”

Each party will aim to reshape government funding along its priorities in the fight for full-year bills after the midterms are decided. Another CR moving the deadline into the new year is likely, especially if Democrats retake one or both chambers.

Democrats, if they win back power, will likely seek to downsize defense spending; boost domestic programs for infrastructure, education, childcare and other priorities; and rein in the Trump administration’s powers, including cuts to executive agency staffing and federal spending in general.

Republicans might try to move full-year appropriations bills. But they’ll need Democratic support to do so, and the two parties are still far apart on spending totals.

House Republicans have passed just three full-year funding bills so far, while Senate negotiators have yet to reach a deal on a top-line spending number. Democrats will have even less motivation to cooperate with Republicans in the short term if they are expecting to retake the majority next year.

articles.title: GOP senator ‘disappointed’ over departure of Army secretary who clashed with Hegseth
articles.summary: Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.), a senior Republican on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he was “disappointed” to learn of the resignation of Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll and expressed concern about the broader turnover of senior military officers under Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. “I was disappointed. I think he’s been a pretty solid guy.…
articles.body:
Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.), a senior Republican on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he was “disappointed” to learn of the resignation of Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll and expressed concern about the broader turnover of senior military officers under Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

“I was disappointed. I think he’s been a pretty solid guy. So disappointed,” Rounds said of Discroll’s departure from the Army after clashing with Hegseth over the ouster of key senior officials, such as Gen. Randy George, who served as the Army’s chief of staff, and Christopher Donahue, the top U.S. Army commander in Europe.

Rounds said he understood Driscoll’s departure was linked to disagreements over the firing or forced resignation of senior leaders under Hegseth.

“I’m hearing the same rumors everybody else is that he was frustrated with some of his top generals being released. That’s not the first time I’ve heard that. I think that points to questions that we’re going to be asking when we get back,” Rounds said, referring to the questions senators will have of Hegseth and Pentagon leaders about turmoil at the Pentagon.

The Senate is in the midst of a five-week recess and is scheduled to reconvene in Washington on Sept. 14.

“Where’s the leadership at? We’ve had some very good generals that are no longer there that we respected and had a huge amount of foundational knowledge in terms of moving us forward as far as the changing capabilities we need to incorporate in the fighting force,” Rounds said.

GOP senators have expressed concern over the departure of senior officials, such as George, for months.

Driscoll, an Iraq War veteran and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance, championed the development of a drone warfare initiative to learn lessons from the drone-intensive fighting from the Ukrainian-Russian war.

That initiative was shut down by acting Army Chief of Staff Christopher LaNeve. LaNeve ordered special European battalion specializing in drone warfare to refocus on its core mission of being an airborne infantry unit, according to the Associated Press .

Rounds questioned the effort by some senior officials viewed as more aligned with Hegseth to shut down efforts to develop new strategies and tactics for drone warfare by pointing out that drone-intensive tactics appears to be a significant and lasting evolution of military doctrine.

“This issue that’s going on with regard to Ukraine, the use of drones, the integration of drones into this — this is not a new thing that just happened. We’ve been watching this ever since 2021. … Watching the Ukrainians do a marvelous job with drones. We’ve been watching this,” he said.

Rounds also talked about the importance of the “integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into our offensive and our defensive capabilities.”

“We know that our adversaries are doing it right now and the question is, ‘Are we keeping up with them?’ ‘Are they keeping up with us?’ But we’ve got real serious issues there that we need to be able to fund and direct and those are things we can’t wait six months to do,” he added.

Asked if he still has confidence in Hegseth’s leadership, Rounds said that question is entirely up to President Trump.

“It’s not a matter or not of whether we are. It’s a matter of whether the president is” confident in Hegseth’s leadership, he said.

“The president chooses who he wants for his key leaders. I think they’re trying. We want to see results,” he said.

GOP lawmakers are growing increasingly frustrated with Hegseth’s leadership of the Defense Department as the war with Iran has dragged on for six months now with no clear end in sight.

The White House will host a press briefing on Thursday, marking the first briefing in over 40 days.

A White House official who confirmed the plans did not specify who would be briefing the press.

News of the upcoming briefing comes days after former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt wrapped up her final day in the role. Leavitt will continue to serve as an outside adviser to President Trump and will work with his super PAC MAGA Inc.

When Leavitt went on a roughly monthlong maternity leave earlier this year, a cast of characters from the administration took to the podium to brief the press, including Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

It’s unclear who will replace Leavitt, but a number of names have been floated. Potential contenders include CNN commentator Scott Jennings and former U.S. Attorney for the district of New Jersey Alina Habba.

Trump has given no indication he is in a rush to replace Leavitt, who said on her final day as press secretary that the president is “his own best spokesperson.”

articles.title: MapQuest tops Apple, Google Maps in downloads after refusing Trump’s ‘Lake America’ change
articles.summary: MapQuest has surged in popularity on the app charts after the mapping service said it would not rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” after President Trump signed an executive order changing its name. The company said its mobile app received hundreds of thousands of downloads after it announced Thursday that the name Lake Ontario would…
articles.body:
MapQuest has surged in popularity on the app charts after the mapping service said it would not rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” after President Trump signed an executive order changing its name.

The company said its mobile app received hundreds of thousands of downloads after it announced Thursday that the name Lake Ontario would remain on its apps , despite Trump directing the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

By Monday morning, MapQuest had climbed to No. 1 among navigation apps in Apple’s U.S. app store and No. 4 in non-gaming apps. In Canada, which shares the lake with the U.S., the app reached No. 2 overall over the weekend.

The app’s usage also jumped to roughly 50 times its normal level, according to MapQuest.

MapQuest responded similarly to the controversy surrounding Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in office, allowing its users to refer to the body of water however they please.

“We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they’re familiar with,” Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest, said in a statement .

“Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app,” he added.

The move contrasts the approach taken by competitor Google Maps, which began displaying Lake America for U.S. users on Saturday after the name was added to the GNIS. Canadians will continue to see Lake Ontario, in line with opposition from Canadian leaders to refer to it as Lake America, while users elsewhere will see both names.

Apple Maps continues to display the lake as Lake Ontario as of Tuesday morning. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Monday that Trump had reached out to Apple directly about changing the name on its mapping services.

Trump signed an executive order last week formally changing the U.S. government’s designation for Lake Ontario amid an escalating trade war with Canada after negotiations collapsed between the longtime allies.

Canadian officials have pushed back on Trump’s move to rename the Great Lake, asserting that it will not adopt the new name.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Sunday that the name change resembled “something out of ‘Saturday Night Live,’” while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney cited the lake’s longstanding history as a reason to reject the change.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney said. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

articles.title: Two Democrats, in highly unusual move, cross the aisle to save GOP bills
articles.summary: Two Democrats took the unusual step of voting with Republicans to advance a batch of GOP-backed bills, preventing a handful of conservatives from tanking the vote and effectively saving Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) agenda for the week. The rule was adopted 210-208, with five Republicans voting in opposition and two Democrats — Reps. Jared Golden…
articles.body:
Two Democrats took the unusual step of voting with Republicans to advance a batch of GOP-backed bills, preventing a handful of conservatives from tanking the vote and effectively saving Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) agenda for the week.

The rule was adopted 210-208, with five Republicans voting in opposition and two Democrats — Reps. Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) — voting in favor.

The rule includes a GOP-backed bill to denounce socialism, a key midterm message for Republicans.

Golden and Perez’s votes were highly unconventional. Traditionally, the majority party votes in favor of rules, which tee up debate and final votes on bills, while the minority party votes against them, regardless of how lawmakers plan to vote on the underlying legislation.

In the razor-thin GOP majority this Congress, conservatives have frequently used rule votes to flex their muscles and push for their positions, but a member of the minority party crossing the aisle in this way is near-unheard of.

The votes blindsided Democratic leaders, who said they hadn’t gotten any advance notice from Perez or Golden.

“That came as a surprise,” Democratic Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) said shortly after the vote.

Clark said she has not spoken to the lawmakers since they cast their votes, but she was clearly frustrated with the pair for violating the precedent around rule votes.

“It’s one of the rules of being on a team, is that we vote against the rule. So I’m sure we’ll have further discussions,” Clark said.

The conservatives who voted against the rule did so to protest a measure not included in it, the Senate-crafted continuing resolution (CR) to fund the government through Dec. 11, which contains provisions a number of House conservatives opposed. But the CR passed Tuesday under suspension of the rules, depriving them of the opportunity to block it.

That group included: Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.), Clay Higgins (R-La.), Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), Chip Roy (R-Texas) and Pete Sessions (R-Texas).

Roy, who had vowed Monday to vote against the rule, said the detractors weren’t trying to win others over.

“People asked us what we thought. We told them. Andy and I both felt strongly about the fact that they were amending the CR. You didn’t get the CR in the rule, but you know, people got to vote however they want to,” he said. “So we weren’t like having a big push to try to you know quote kill the rule. I just I wasn’t going to support it.”

Higgins also bashed the Senate for adding provisions to the CR.

“Well, I mean, we’re leaning in on on the non-performance of the Senate. That’s what’s really happening,” he said. “These guys across campus, they act like the royal court over there.”

articles.title: Democratic leaders blindsided by two members who bailed out Johnson
articles.summary: House Democratic leaders were blindsided by the two rank-and-file members who crossed the aisle on Tuesday to help Republicans advance a series of GOP messaging bills heading into the midterm elections. Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), the Democratic whip, said she received no advance notice from either Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) or Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez…
articles.body:
House Democratic leaders were blindsided by the two rank-and-file members who crossed the aisle on Tuesday to help Republicans advance a series of GOP messaging bills heading into the midterm elections.

Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), the Democratic whip, said she received no advance notice from either Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) or Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) that they intended to support a Republican rule governing the GOP bills.

“That came as a surprise,” Clark said shortly after the vote.

Clark said she has not spoken to the lawmakers since they cast their votes, but she was clearly frustrated with the pair for flouting an unwritten rule of House politics: The minority party virtually always unites against the majority party’s rules, even if members of the minority support the underlying legislation.

“It’s one of the rules of being on a team, is that we vote against the rule. So I’m sure we’ll have further discussions,” Clark said.

Asked if that would include any disciplinary measures, she steered clear.

“We’ll just have further discussions,” Clark said.

The aggravation emerged just as Democratic leaders were optimistic they could block the rule underlying a series of GOP messaging bills before the House leaves Washington to hit the campaign trail.

Among the bills are legislation to condemn socialism, punish universities that boycott Israel, and to amend protections for the North Atlantic right whale.

Five conservative Republicans voted against the rule, not because they oppose the underlying bills but as a protest against the decision by GOP leaders to pass a massive government funding bill without going through the normal rules process. That strategy allowed Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to adopt the Senate-passed funding bill, known as a continuing resolution (CR), with broad bipartisan support, thereby avoiding a politically perilous government shutdown.

Those five GOP dissenters would have been enough to sink the rule on the Republican messaging bills if the Democrats had stayed united in opposition. Instead, the support from Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez put the measure over the top.

Golden has sponsored a version of one of the underlying bills, which is designed to protect lobstermen from economic harm due to the protections for the right whale.

articles.title: Lancaster coroner investigating child measles death amid Trump admin scrutiny
articles.summary: The Lancaster coroner’s office is investigating the second case of a child who reportedly died after testing positive for measles as the state faces scrutiny from the Trump administration about the death. Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni confirmed the second diagnosis Tuesday and said his office was “in the process of doing an investigation.” The…
articles.body:
The Lancaster coroner’s office is investigating the second case of a child who reportedly died after testing positive for measles as the state faces scrutiny from the Trump administration about the death.

Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni confirmed the second diagnosis Tuesday and said his office was “in the process of doing an investigation.”

The coroner’s office will release the cause of death following the conclusion of the investigation, which could take weeks.

The investigation comes a week after Pennsylvania’s Department of Health confirmed in a release that two unvaccinated residents in Lancaster County died from contracting measles, though county officials are unsure if this second case is related to the state’s announcement.

Diamantoni said that he “can’t tell you with certainty this is the death the Department of Health and governor’s office was referring to.”

“We just want to cast as wide a net as possible and identify any deaths that may have occurred in individuals who had measles,” the coroner stated.

Lancaster Commissioner Josh Parsons also confirmed on social media Tuesday that the county coroner’s office “has been working to identify the case” of measles in the state because “the state has still provided zero information on the second case.”

The first death Diamantoni investigated was a newborn baby who his office determined died from measles.

“The forensic pathologist at the autopsy determined the cause of death was the result of a laceration of the spleen and subsequent bleeding,” the coroner added.

The deaths reported by the state and county mark the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in 35 years and the first in the country this year.

Trump administration health officials have disputed claims made by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) that these deaths were related to vaccine misinformation.

Shapiro said at a press conference when the deaths were announced that, “there’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids.”

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. responded in an Aug. 25 post , saying, “The Trump administration is working to restore public trust not by gaslighting or manipulating, but by being truthful, at last, with the public.”

“During our phone conversation, Governor Shapiro also accused me of promoting vaccine misinformation,” Kennedy continued. “As I told him, HHS does not tolerate misinformation by any employee.”

Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, even questioned the cause of death in an interview Thursday.

“We don’t know if the children died from measles or had another condition that was already attacking them and they happened to get measles at the same time,” he said.

The Lancaster county coroner’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment on the ongoing investigation.

articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) commented Tuesday on President Trump making him the “main character” of this year’s midterms, saying the move may give the Democrat a “gigantic platform” should he win in November.

“Trump is messing around and making me the … front page or the main character of the midterms,” El-Sayed told Michiganders on the campaign trail, as captured on C-SPAN cameras.

“That allows me then to both move a conversation but also maneuver inside because I can move a conversation across,” the candidate added.

Trump has repeatedly blasted El-Sayed after the Senate hopeful knocked off Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the Wolverine State’s Democratic primary last month. The progressive Democrat is set to face off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in November.

During an event in Las Vegas, the day after Michigan’s primaries, the president called El-Sayed a “man of hate” who “hates Jews and hates Israel.” In subsequent Truth Social posts , Trump labeled the progressive Democrat “crazy,” a “jihadist” and a “dumocrat,” among other insults.

“He’s a man of hate, and now he’s going around saying, ‘Oh I love everybody.’ He doesn’t love everybody,” the president said his Las Vegas speech. “Put him in office, and you’re going to find out what he loves.”

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed has criticized the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. The former Wayne County health official has also argued the U.S. government should forgo involvement in foreign conflicts in favor of investing more in social services at home.

Earlier this week, Vice President Vance labeled El-Sayed as “evil,” saying he is “fighting for one group at the expense of others.” El-Sayed, who is Muslim, was born in Rochester Hills, Mich., to Egyptian immigrant parents.

El-Sayed doubled down on his talking points while speaking to Michiganders on Tuesday, saying his views on international affairs are informed by his preference to keep tax dollars in the U.S.

“That money is money that’s being spent in the West Bank, that should be spent on the West Side [of Detroit],” he said, referring to the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

El-Sayed added, “One of the things you’ll hear me talk about all the time is, I don’t want to fight stupid wars. I want to invest … in infrastructure, water infrastructure being one of those things.”

Polling indicates the El-Sayed-Rogers race will be tight, as the two fight to succeed outgoing Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

A survey EPIC-MIRA conducted in late August found that 47 percent of respondents backed or leaned toward El-Sayed, while 43 percent supported or leaned toward Rogers . The poll had a margin of error of 4 percentage points.

As of Monday, Decision Desk HQ gave El-Sayed a 68 percent chance of winning.

articles.title: Allies of disgraced ex-House Dem poised for criminal charges for refusing Congress' probe
articles.summary: Allies of a former House Democrat face DOJ criminal charges after the House unanimously held them in contempt of Congress over defied subpoenas.
articles.body: Allies of a former House Democrat under federal indictment are now facing potential criminal charges themselves. The House of Representatives unanimously agreed to hold two people in contempt of Congress on Tuesday — North Miami Beach, Florida, Mayor Michael Joseph and Hector Roos, a former aide to ex-Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, D-Fla. — for failing to work with the House Ethics Committee's investigation into the disgraced Sunshine State Democrat. It's now up to the Department of Justice (DOJ) whether it pursues criminal charges against both. A contempt of Congress conviction carries a fine of up to $100,000 and up to a year in jail. DISGRACED DEM CUT OFF FROM DOING BUSINESS WITH GOVERNMENT AFTER ALLEGED ‘OUTRIGHT FRAUD’ UNCOVERED "The committee cannot fulfill its obligations to safeguard the integrity of the House for witnesses, ignore its subpoenas, and the House cannot accept such willful disregard of its authorities. Mr. Roos and Mr. Joseph willfully fail to comply with multiple subpoenas issued by the committee," Committee Chairman Michael Guest, R-Miss., said. "They impeded the investigative subcommittee's investigations into the allegations concerning former Representative Cherfilus-McCormick. Those allegations were serious and included violations of federal law to which Mr. Roos and Mr. Joseph were party there. Their conduct warrants referrals to the United States Department of Justice for contempt of Congress." MIKE JOHNSON SAYS HE SUPPORTS EXPELLING SHEILA CHERFILUS-MCCORMICK OVER DOZENS OF ETHICS VIOLATIONS The measure passed by voice vote on Tuesday afternoon, meaning lawmakers were not individually put on the record over where they stand. Any lawmaker can stand and object to a voice vote and call for a roll call instead, which none did. The Democrats present instead signaled they were fully in support of the bid against their fellow left-wingers. FLORIDA DEM FILED FOR RE-ELECTION DAYS BEFORE RESIGNATION AS HOUSE ETHICS COMMITTEE RAMPED UP PRESSURE "At a time when public confidence in Congress is at historic lows and the House's ability to self-police member conduct is under intense scrutiny, enforcing lawful congressional process is vital to delivering swift transparency and accountability for any misconduct," Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said. "A witness who refuses to cooperate with the Ethics Committee hinders the thoroughness and swiftness of an investigation." Guest charged that Roos "filed inaccurate reports" with the Federal Election Commission while working for Cherfilus-McCormick. He said Roos did not provide adequate justification for not complying with the committee. "Mr. Joseph was the president of a company that improperly provided corporate funds for the congresswoman's campaign, influenced her staff to submit community funding project requests for entities that he supported," Guest said of the other target. He said Joseph cited attorney-client privilege in his decision not to comply with the committee, but that lawmakers argued it was not a valid justification to dodge the probe. INDICTED DEMOCRAT SHEILA CHERFILUS-MCCORMICK REFUSES TO RESIGN AS EXPULSION VOTE LOOMS Cherfilus-McCormick resigned from Congress earlier this year amid intense pressure from both the left and right. Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., had been threatening to push a resolution to expel her at the time. articles.body:
Former Mesa County, Colorado elections clerk Tina Peters turned down a job offer to oversee elections in a conservative California county north of Sacramento, the Los Angeles Times reported Tuesday.

“She declined the offer because she’s running around the country right now trying to secure the elections,” Shasta County, Ca. registrar of voters Clint Curtis told the outlet. “Shasta County lost out.”

The Hill has reached out to the registrar of voters for comment.

Curtis, who has made claims about rigged voting machines since the early 2000s, told the LA Times that he sought Peters out as a consultant “to assist with supervision of the November election.” He described California as a “second-chance state. Except for Peters.”

“No second chance for her in Shasta County,” he told the newspaper.

Peters’s lawyer, Peter Ticktin, told the Times that she seriously considered the job but that she would not have served in the role full-time due to her schedule, calling her an “American icon.”

The Shasta County official indicated last month that he wanted to hire her to replace his top deputy on medical leave. Speaking with “The Northstate Breakdown,” he said that Peters had experience and was “able to take the rocks and arrows.”

California Democrats slammed the notion that she would have a role in the Golden State’s elections. Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) called hiring Peters “a disgrace.”

“I’m directing [the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation] to make every effort to BLOCK any transfer of her parole supervision into California,” Newsom wrote on social media on Monday.

Sens. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) on Saturday sent a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber stating their concern has less to do with her qualifications and more to do with President Trump’s “obsession with interfering in the midterm elections.”

Peters previously oversaw the results of the 2020 election while working as an elections clerk in Mesa County, Colo. The votes she certified were found to heavily favor Trump, but former President Biden won the state by 13 points, prompting Trump to later claim Democrats had “stolen” his victory.

Peters was later charged in connection with providing an associate of MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, who has also made false remarks about the integrity of the 2020 election, with access to the county’s voter systems in search of alleged fraud in May 2021.

She was found guilty on seven counts, including four felony counts for election interference, and sentenced to nine years in prison. But in April, a Colorado appeals court ruled that Peters should be resentenced, resulting in her release after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence.

Trump, who would post on Truth Social calls to “FREE TINA,” pressured Polis to pardon her after the president gave her a symbolic pardon in 2025.

Colorado Democrats censured Polis for the commutation. The governor later reportedly fired two members of his clemency board for publicly opposing the commutation.

articles.title: Spanberger fact-checked after Trump mail-voting warning raises military ballot fears
articles.summary: CNN issued a correction after Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Wolf Blitzer suggested Trump's mail-voting rules could impact military voters abroad.
articles.body: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger claimed the Trump administration was attempting to take away the ability of Americans serving overseas to vote by mail — despite the Postal Service’s final rule explicitly exempting military and overseas ballots from its new requirements. The Postal Service’s (USPS) final rule at the center of the dispute expressly exempts ballots covered by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) from the new federal ballot-mail requirements — though an Obama-appointed federal judge temporarily stayed key provisions of the rule Thursday. "If you are serving our country abroad, I believe that you should have the ability to cast a vote in our elections. The Trump Administration is attempting to take that ability away," Spanberger wrote on X on Aug. 29. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS The final rule says UOCAVA voters are excluded and explains that the separate treatment reflects the circumstances facing military personnel, their families and other overseas voters. Spanberger made a similar argument during a CNN interview after anchor Wolf Blitzer raised the possibility that Virginia military personnel overseas could be affected. CNN subsequently returned on air to clarify that UOCAVA ballots are exempt from the new USPS requirements. "The continued attacks that we're seeing from the Trump administration [are] really just an effort to get people fearful, to get to stay home, and in many cases, to eliminate what is a valid, safe, secure way for people to be able to make their voices heard and to vote," she said. Blitzer added that Virginia is home to "a lot of military personnel who totally rely on mail-in ballots if they want to be able to express their opinion." Spanberger agreed, pointing to members of the military and diplomatic services, saying the administration’s actions were impacting them along with other Virginians who find vote-by-mail "a better option." TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS Spanberger did not respond to a request for comment, but when reached, a representative for CNN said Blitzer issued an on-air correction Monday. "On Friday, I interviewed the Democratic governor of Virginia, Abigail Spanberger. We discussed legal challenges to the Trump administration's directives for the Postal Service on mail-in voting," Blitzer said in the correction. "A comment that may’ve suggested that U.S. military and overseas voters' ballots would be impacted by these directives -- I want to be clear right now, those ballots are exempt from the Postal Service's new rules implementing the president's March executive order. Those groups are covered under [UOCAVA], just to be specific on that point." An X community note added as an appendix to Spanberger's tweet of her exchange with Blitzer also surfaced the correction. "Military and overseas voters' UOCAVA ballots are explicitly exempt from the USPS rules implementing the March 2026 executive order; service members abroad can still register/request absentee ballots via the Federal Post Card Application," it read. Several users also pushed back and cited federal statute as well as the USPS’ own rule. Others said the governor was allegedly "lying" and suggested she should know of UOCAVA as a former CIA officer. Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, picked up on her original tweet, responding that he had personally discussed overseas military voting with Trump "many times" and said Trump had consistently made clear he did not want to interfere with Americans serving abroad voting by mail. "This is completely false," Lee tweeted. 2028 DEM HOPEFUL SLAPS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WITH LAWSUIT OVER MAIL-IN VOTING AFTER MAJOR SCOTUS VICTORY The Supreme Court in August handed Trump a largely favorable procedural ruling, staying an earlier injunction after finding that the states’ challenge was premature at that stage. The ruling did not decide the legality of the administration’s mail-voting policies on the merits. America First Legal President Gene Hamilton previously told Fox News Digital that the court prevented the administration from being effectively "enjoined from thinking" before agencies had settled on concrete policies. articles.title: Florida orders removal of Flock cameras from state highways
articles.summary: Florida is halting the use of automated license plate readers (LPRs), including Flock Safety’s controversial cameras, on state highways, its transportation department announced Monday. The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) said in a memo to local law enforcement agencies that they should “cease the issuance of all future requests for LPR systems within its jurisdictional…
articles.body:
Florida is halting the use of automated license plate readers (LPRs), including Flock Safety’s controversial cameras, on state highways, its transportation department announced Monday.

The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) said in a memo to local law enforcement agencies that they should “cease the issuance of all future requests for LPR systems within its jurisdictional authority.”

The order comes as a growing number of jurisdictions throughout the country, including the entire state of Texas , move to restrict the technology. Flock cameras specifically have remained at the helm of this controversy after reports of law enforcement officers’ misuse of their data came to light.

“The recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life,” FDOT wrote Monday.

The order would apply to cameras on the Sunshine State’s highway system — leaving their use on city and county roads up to local officials’ discretion.

As of Tuesday afternoon, local sheriff’s offices in Putnam and Clay counties have already moved to remove all LPRs from their jurisdictions’ roadways.

“Over the past several weeks, legitimate questions have continued to emerge regarding privacy, data sharing, governmental oversight and the future regulation of this technology,” Putnam County Sheriff H.D. DeLoach said in a Monday statement. “I believe the responsible course is to discontinue our program and cancel our contract at this time.”

LPRs at Flock, specifically, offer a system of AI-enabled video cameras and audio detection devices that not only record license plate numbers, but collect specific details about a car to create what the company calls a “vehicle signature.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) expressed concerns surrounding the technology following FDOTs block, saying in a Monday press conference the decision to restrict LPRs would keep the Sunshine State from becoming a “digital AI surveillance state where everything we’re doing is being tracked at all times.”

“If you want to get in your car and you want to go down to Buc-ee’s in St. Augustine, it’s really none of the government’s damn business if you’re doing that, right,” he said. “I know you can make money selling cameras, but you can really make a lot of money selling people’s data.”

The governor also called for the state lawmakers to introduce legislation on LPRs, adding that the memo could be revoked by the gubernatorial candidate who replaces him in January.

Other local officials are criticizing FDOT’s expedited timeline to remove these cameras. Miami Beach Mayor Steven Meiner, for example, told WLRN that “this blanket ban” would “have serious consequences for public safety.”

The growing scrutiny around LPRs has reached more than 150 cities who have made similar moves to cancel or reject LPRs as of Tuesday , according to antisurveillance organization . DeFlock

Flock and Axon, another top LPR producer, did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comments.

articles.body:
Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton are duking it out for the Democratic nod in the Massachusetts Senate race.

Moulton has made the race about generational change, arguing it’s time for “a new generation of leadership.” Markey has held the seat since 2013 and has served in Congress for a total of five decades.

Markey is backed by progressive powerhouses, including Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), while Moulton has notched support from New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D), among others.

John Deaton, who was the 2024 Senate Republican nominee, will take on the winner of Tuesday’s primary. The seat is almost certainly to remain in Democrats’ hands in November.

articles.title: What to watch in Massachusetts: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. Welcome to September! We may be nine weeks away from the general election, but we’re still not done with primary season. In today’s edition, Bridget Bowman and Ben Kamisar break down the key races to watch in Massachusetts. Plus, Natasha Korecki gives us a Chicago history lesson. — Adam Wollner Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here. Massachusetts primary puts Democrats’ generational divides on display By Bridget Bowman and Ben Kamisar Today’s primaries in Massachusetts have turned into the latest battlefield in the Democratic Party’s generational divide, with several longtime legislators facing off against younger challengers. Here are the races to watch. Massachusetts Senate: 80-year-old Democratic Sen. Ed Markey is trying to fend off a primary challenge from 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton. The matchup comes six years after Markey defeated another Democrat more than 30 years his junior, then-Rep. Joe Kennedy III by 11 points. As Steve Kornacki noted in his “Data Dive” newsletter, an electorate that was heavy on college graduates provided Markey with a critical boost in that primary. Moulton is betting that a lot has changed since 2020, particularly with President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory fueling new levels of angst and thirst for change within the Democratic Party. But Markey is looking to tap into the energy on the left that has buoyed progressives in primaries across the country this year. Massachusetts’ 8th District: Rep. Stephen Lynch, 71, is seeking his 14th term in Congress. But Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old former aide to former Gov. Deval Patrick, is pushing Lynch from the left, outraising the incumbent and outspending him significantly on the airwaves. Lynch has rankled progressives over the years, breaking with the majority of his party on votes including the passage of the Affordable Care Act and, more recently, the Laken Riley Act, an immigration detention measure. Massachusetts’ 1st District: Rep. Richard Neal, 77, is also facing a progressive challenge from 39-year-old high school teacher Jeromie Whalen. Neal is the top Democrat on the powerful House Ways and Means Committee and was first elected to Congress in 1988. Read more → 🎥 Tune in to the Kornacki Cam at 7:45 p.m. ET to watch Steve break down tonight’s results. JB Pritzker, Chicago violence and the myth of Malört Analysis by Natasha Korecki CHICAGO — In old-school Chicago, the pattern went something like this: legendary newspaper columnist Mike Royko walked into the Billy Goat Tavern, called out, “Hey, kid,” and bartender Bouchaib Khribech headed over. Khribech poured Royko’s drink of choice: vodka on the rocks. What he wasn’t drinking: Malört. “Sometimes he [would] do a scotch. He was a vodka guy. Malört never existed back then,” Khribech said of the beloved, late Pulitzer Prize winner. One wouldn’t know it from national coverage, the late-night TV show riffs and, most recently, an event featuring Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker that the bitter drink that’s been likened to turpentine, vomit and pencil shavings (I’d go with gasoline) wasn’t always some iconic staple being tossed back in secret rooms. It has been around, yes, but it was obscure. Some grizzled Chicagoans write off the Malört phenomenon as a meme that only recently exploded in popularity. “Richard M. or Richard J. [Daley] — I doubt either one of them ever had Malört. They were Old Style kind of guys,” said Abdon Pallasch, a former longtime political reporter for the Chicago Sun-Times, who went on to work for the state and is now a courts spokesman. (He’s also a former colleague of mine). “In the smoke-filled back rooms of Chicago, people are drinking bourbon or Irish whiskey. Malört wasn’t a thing.” Malört is in the political spotlight after on Sunday Pritzker poured shots at the Recess Bar in the city’s West Loop, as nearly 2,000 people gathered to set a Guiness World Record for the most shots of the drink taken simultaneously. Images inundated social media as the two-term governor poured shots from behind the bar, and tilted the bottle back for a swig. As a billionaire who has his sights set on 2028 — and more immediately, re-election in November — the “everyman” image may not hurt. The event drew goodwill, energy and benefitted charity. But the timing of it, the same weekend the city experienced one of the most violent weekends this summer with 41 people shot and three killed, opened Pritzker to some negative coverage. Pritzker addressed the violence and held a labor event on Sunday in the area where a mass shooting had taken place the prior night. At the same time, President Donald Trump, who last year tried to take credit for a marked drop in Chicago crime, which began its slide before he took office, now puts the blame for a 1% year-over-year rise in homicides squarely on Pritzker. He said he would send federal law enforcement but needed local officials to ask him. “I am awaiting the call. Nobody should be forced to live under these conditions,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Like D.C. and others, they will have almost no crime, FAST! The State and City can’t do what I do. Governor Pritzker, CALL!!!” In a post on X, Pritzker noted that the Trump administration slashed anti-violence funding efforts in Chicago in 2025. Last year’s immigration deployment in the city also stirred violent clashes. “When Trump last sent agents to Illinois, they murdered a father and shot an innocent woman in broad daylight — then attempted to cover it up,” Pritzker wrote. “We need to keep reducing violence, but this President does not make it easier. If only he hadn’t defunded the very programs that help.” Beyond that, a Pritzker spokesman took issue with criticism of the Malört event. “In the age of social media where you can barely verify if an actual human or a Russian bot is posting, the press should treat criticism from a few loud online voices with more skepticism,” Pritzker spokesman Matt Hill said. “If there wasn’t this double standard, then we would anticipate seeing more stories about all the time President Trump spends doomscrolling and golfing.” That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola.
